title: Finitely many maximal points of a Noetherian vanishing topos
statement: Let $S$ be a Noetherian scheme, meaning locally Noetherian [pqf-def-locnoeth] and quasi-compact [def-weil-pbc-quasi-compact-scheme], and let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of finite presentation [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]. Let $V_f$ be the vanishing topos [def-trf-oriented-nearby-cycles]. A point is a geometric morphism $p:\mathbf{Set}\to V_f$ [def-trf-geometric-morphism]. Write $p\leq q$ if there is a $2$-morphism $q\Rightarrow p$, equivalently a natural transformation $p^{-1}\Rightarrow q^{-1}$ of fibre functors. The isomorphism classes of points have finitely many maximal elements for this order, and every point $p$ admits such a $2$-morphism from a representative of a maximal class. Maximality and finiteness here concern isomorphism classes, not a choice of geometric fields.

source.place: Author draft, Lemma 8.3.2 and preceding definition of the point order, printed p. 18; finite-presentation specialization of its finite-type alternative. No excellence hypothesis is imposed.

proof.text: For a point $p$ of $V_f$, compose with the two projections. By [lem-trf-etale-topos-points-geometric] these two points are represented by geometric points $\bar x$ of $X$ and $\bar t$ of $S$. The structural $2$-morphism, conjugated by these identifications, is $u:\bar t\Rightarrow f\bar x$. The universal property in [lem-trf-oriented-product-universal] identifies $p$ with the triple $(\bar x,\bar t,u)$. Write $t$ for its second underlying scheme point. If $q\Rightarrow p$, evaluate the inverse-image natural transformation on $p_2^{-1}U$ for each open $U\subseteq S$. Its values are empty or singleton, so every open containing $t(p)$ contains $t(q)$. Thus $t(p)\in\overline{\{t(q)\}}$.

source.place: Section 1, point-triple description; Section 8.3, order definition immediately before Lemma 8.3.2.

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finitely-many-components], [lem-sc-irreducible-components-cover] and [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-sober], choose the finitely many component generic points $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_r$ of $S$; every $t\in S$ is a specialization of some $\eta_i$. For $p=(\bar x,\bar t,u)$ choose such an $i$ and a geometric point $\bar\eta_i$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-specialization-strict-local-lift] to $\eta_i\leadsto t$ to lift $\bar\eta_i$ into $S_{(\bar t)}$. Each pointed etale neighbourhood of $\bar t$ consequently has a compatible lift of $\bar\eta_i$; taking germs gives a natural transformation of set-valued stalks $\bar t^{-1}\to\bar\eta_i^{-1}$, hence a $2$-morphism $\gamma:\bar\eta_i\Rightarrow\bar t$. Put $p'=(\bar x,\bar\eta_i,u\gamma)$. The fibre formula in [lem-trf-oriented-product-universal] constructs $p'\Rightarrow p$: on a triple generator its inverse-image mate sends $(a,b)$ to $(a,\gamma^{-1}(b))$, where $\gamma^{-1}$ denotes the inverse-image mate, not an inverse map. The fibre-product equation is preserved by naturality. This construction is compatible with all arrows of triples and hence defines the natural transformation on sheaves. Thus every point is below one whose second support is one of the $\eta_i$.

source.place: First sentence of the proof of Lemma 8.3.2; lifting is Stacks etale-cohomology.tex Tag 0GJ5, remark-can-lift.

proof.text: For any $s\in S$, form $Y_s=X\times_SN_s$ as in [lem-trf-oriented-point-normalized-stratum]. That statement identifies isomorphism classes with second support $s$, with the relation induced from the whole $V_f$, with the Zariski generization order on $Y_s$. In particular it asserts antisymmetry on this stratum. If $p\leq q$ and $q\leq p$ in $V_f$, Step 1 gives equal closures of their second supports. Schemes are sober by [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-sober], so these supports coincide, say at $s$. The antisymmetry just cited then gives $[p]=[q]$. Identities and composition give reflexivity and transitivity. Hence the relation in the statement really is a partial order on point isomorphism classes, not merely a preorder.

source.place: Order definition before Lemma 8.3.2 and its proof, identification with the Zariski order after normalization.

proof.text: Finite presentation of $f$ in [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] implies finite type: each finitely presented affine coordinate algebra is finitely generated, and quasi-compactness is already part of finite presentation. For each $\eta_i$, [lem-trf-normalized-base-change-noetherian-topology] therefore makes $|Y_{\eta_i}|$ a Noetherian topological space; it does not assert that $N_{\eta_i}$ has Noetherian local rings. By [lem-sc-noetherian-finite-irreducible-components] this space has finitely many irreducible components. By [lem-sc-irreducible-components-cover] they cover it, and by [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-sober] each has a generic point. Every point of $Y_{\eta_i}$ is consequently a specialization of one of those finitely many generic points. Under [lem-trf-oriented-point-normalized-stratum], their classes form a finite subset $C_i$ of the point classes of $V_f$ that dominates every class with second support $\eta_i$. Empty $Y_{\eta_i}$ simply contributes $C_i=\varnothing$.

source.place: Proof of Lemma 8.3.2, normalization and final finite-type alternative, followed by its Zariski-order identification.

proof.text: Let $C=\bigcup_{i=1}^r C_i$, removing any repeated isomorphism classes. It is finite. Step 2 puts an arbitrary class $[p]$ below a class in some $\eta_i$-stratum, and Step 4 puts that class below an element of $C$. Composition shows that $C$ dominates every point class. For each $c\in C$ choose a maximal element $m$ of the finite ordered subset $\{d\in C:c\leq d\}$. Such an $m$ exists by successively moving to a strictly larger element; finiteness prevents continuing or repeating a class. It is maximal in the entire point order: if $m\leq z$, choose $d\in C$ with $z\leq d$ by the domination property. Then $c\leq m\leq d$, so maximality in that finite subset gives $d=m$, and antisymmetry gives $z=m$. Thus every point is below a maximal class. Conversely a maximal class $z$ is below some $d\in C$, and hence equals $d$. All maximal classes therefore lie in the finite set $C$. Each inequality is witnessed by a $2$-morphism, and their composites give the required morphism from a maximal representative to $p$. This also treats the empty topos: the empty $C$ then has no classes to dominate.

source.place: Conclusion of Lemma 8.3.2; explicit finite-cofinal-poset argument for both assertions.
